lessons.title: Sort, match and order
lessons.goal: Sort collections and compare small sets.
lessons.look: Aishatu's toy shop is open. The club needs to tidy leaf tickets and top counters for a new game. Mr Aliyu helps them sort and compare.
lessons.learn: A set is a collection. Sort by one rule: leaves together and tops together. Match one leaf to one top. Unmatched tops show which set has more. Sets with a partner for every object have the same number. Count sets and put them in order from fewest to most.
lessons.worked: Match 2 tops to 4 tops, one to one. Two tops in the set of 4 have no partner. Four is more than two; two is fewer than four. Sets of 2, 3 and 4 go in that order from fewest to most.
lessons.play: Sort clean, large leaves and large tops into separate sets. Match one leaf to one top. Say which set has more, fewer, or the same number. Swap roles. Make sets of 1 to 5 tops and order them from fewest to most.
lessons.hint: Read aloud and model sorting before matching. Put one object beside one partner; spacing and object size do not decide which set has more. Provide reachable materials and allow pointing, speaking or moving objects. Recheck later with fresh sets.

pages.title: Teach, notice and return
pages.subtitle: P1-02 / Sort, match and order / Mr Aliyu leads.

elements.text: Objective. Sort collections and compare small sets. Also retain the source ordering practice within 1 to 5. Read all pupil text aloud. Prerequisite: count objects to five; revisit the Chapter 1 model as needed. The pupil pages have no numbered instructions.

Concrete start. At a reachable table, provide three clean, large leaves and five large, clean tops. Use pieces too large to swallow; supervise use. These are pretend tickets and counters, not food. Sort by type in front of pupils, then invite them to sort a separate tray. A set means a collection. Reuse this same three-leaf/five-top tray for the ending. No pieces are added or removed.

Model, practise, compare. Enact p. 2 with real pieces before using the pictures. On p. 3 pair two tops with four, one to one, and point to the two unmatched tops. Name more and fewer. On the equal-row activity, invite a prediction, then match: all three have partners in both rows, so the sets have the same number even when spaced differently. On p. 4 count the dot sets 2, 3, 4 before connecting them to numerals. Read the numerals aloud.

Observe and help. Confuses type with colour: restate leaves together/tops together, sort one, then ask the child to place another. Counts twice: move each counted object aside. Chooses by row length: bring one object beside one partner. Gives a partner twice: physically move paired objects together. Cannot order: build sets of 1, 3 and 4, then compare adjacent sets. Recheck each difficulty with fresh small sets; accept speaking, pointing or moving objects before writing.

Recall and fresh checks. On p. 6 wait before offering help. After support, change the quantities (for example 1 and 2) and ask again. For this recheck, 2 has more and 1 has fewer. Keep p. 7 fresh tasks independent before feedback. On another day, ask what Mr Aliyu showed. Give four leaves and two tops to sort and compare, then ask pupils to order 5, 2, 3. Answers: leaves/tops; four leaves more, two tops fewer; 2, 3, 5. Record independent / with help / not yet.

elements.text:
Every example and added task
p. 1 tray and p. 2 sort model: 3 leaves and 5 tops. Guided sort: the leaf in the second position is already circled; point to the leaf in the fourth position. Tops are first and third. Grace moves her leaf to the leaves.
p. 3 model: 2 matched pairs, 2 unpaired tops in the four-set; 4 more, 2 fewer. Guided rows: 3 in each, every top has a partner; same number. Any one-to-one bijection is valid.
p. 4 model: 2, 3, 4 dots in increasing order.
p. 6 support: 2 pairs and 1 unmatched lower dot; lower set of 3 has more. Accept either valid line from the remaining upper dot to a free lower dot.
p. 7 resolution: 3 pairs, 2 spare tops; tops more, leaves fewer. Put those 2 unmatched tops in a real spare box. Read the closing dialogue after doing this action.
p. 7 fresh sort: circle second and fourth objects (leaves). Fresh comparison: 5 leaves more than 4 tops; circle the right set.
P1-02-Q2 (p. 4): One dot in one set; three in the other.
P1-02-Q5 (p. 6): Exactly five objects.
P1-02-Q6 (p. 6): Match one to one or count both sets.

Words: sort = group by a rule; set = collection; match = pair one with one; more/fewer = greater/smaller number; same number = no unmatched objects. Historical source: original p. 1; objective/question links retained. Current curriculum comparison and Gombe educator review pending.

elements.text: Sequence. Pupil textbook pages 1-6: classroom purpose; two-to-none demonstration and the meaning of 0; guided one-to-none, recognition, numeral formation and empty-box drawing; independent source tasks; recall/support; actual packing resolution and fresh checks. Use the existing book introductions; this continuation does not repeat them.

Prepare. Large safe counters, reachable tray/mat, storage box, pencil/paper and ordinary cards 0-5. Demonstrate each physical action. The trays/boxes in exact diagrams are containers, not counted tops. Never count decorative classroom artwork. No subtraction or equality notation is needed in these pupil pages.

Notice. Separate empty-set meaning, recognition, independently naming a numeral, and writing without copying. A child may count the tray as one: ask what is being counted, then inspect its contents. An open or reversed loop needs formation practice, not a judgement that the child cannot understand none. Accept usual communication for naming; use an established adapted writing method where needed.

Intervene, then recheck. Use one counter and another container. Model moving it away and checking the contents. Link none to 0. Recheck independently with two counters and a fresh tray, both put away: zero remain. For writing, air-write and trace a large closed loop, cover the model, then dictate zero on blank paper. Give specific feedback and retry later.

Delayed recall. Next session put three counters in a different basket, then ask the pupil to put all away: zero remain. Mix cards 2,0,4: independently name two, zero, four without an adult supplying the names. Cover them and dictate zero: write 0. Record meaning, recognition, naming and formation separately; give further supported practice if needed.

elements.text:
Source questions, unchanged meaning/order.
P1-03-Q1 (TB4/WB1): 0 tops in the empty set.
Q2 (TB4/WB1): a closed box outline with nothing inside; acceptable neat alternatives.
Q3 (TB4/WB2): missing numeral 2 in 0,1,2,3.
Q4 (TB5/WB3): all three put away; 0 remain.
Q5 (TB5/WB3): say zero, using usual communication if needed.
Q6 (TB5/WB3): no oranges are inside the basket; the basket exists.

Models/guided (TB2-3/WB1-2). Two tops before moving, zero after. One top moved away leaves zero. Choose 0 among cards 0,2,1. Closed oval for 0; arrow shows downward direction on the left. Empty-box outline is a model, not a writing space in the textbook. Real quantity sequence none/one/two/three matches 0/1/2/3. WB1 completed example: 1 top, written numeral 1.

Recall/support/ending (TB5-6/WB3). Recall: no objects inside. Support: one then two counters moved away, zero remain. Ending: zero on mat, three stored; actually move counters and check the mat before closure. Count stored objects once each; no objects are lost or added.

Fresh checks (TB6/WB4). Privately prepare trays with 0,2,4 safe counters; change positions. Empty tray contains 0. Write 0 without copying. Shuffle cards 0-5 (no fixed order); ask recognition by naming a card, then independently test reading by pointing without saying its name, including 0 and two other values. Before dictation, cover all cards and earlier written/printed numerals, including the first count answer on WB4. Then dictate zero. WB4 records separate recognition/reading/writing results; repeated tasks on two surfaces are one assessment, not two.
Do not prompt an answer before a naming check. Vary tray positions and card order. Compare observable actions with the rubric; these activities have not been administered to pupils.

elements.text: Words. Empty: nothing inside. None: no objects of the kind being counted. Zero: the number for none. Numeral: a written number symbol. Mat/tray/box: containers or surfaces whose contents we count. An empty box is still a box.

Historical mapping. P1-p01-06: zero as empty collection; -07: read zero; -08: write zero. Stable P1-03-Q1-Q6 preserve source prompts, order and answer meanings; concrete independent empty-set/recognition/naming/formation checks extend the source. Subtraction notation in the legacy worked field is intentionally not used before its prerequisites.

lessons.title: Six to nine
lessons.goal: Count, read, write and order numbers to 9.
lessons.look: Daniel brings more tops to the game. Count on after five together.
lessons.learn: Five and one more make six. Count on: 6, 7, 8, 9. Give one number word to each object. Practise writing 6, 7, 8 and 9.
lessons.play: Sort tops by colour. Make sets of 6, 7, 8 and 9. Swap mats and check. Order the mats from fewest to most.
lessons.hint: Check that 6 and 9 face the correct way. Read numbers as well as copying them.

textbook_pages.title: A place for every piece

elements.text:
Count each one.
Check the group.

Mr Aliyu: Aishatu has made a box game. Its paper pieces are all mixed.
Aishatu: I want to build the game now!
Grace: Let us make neat groups first.
Adamu: Everyone can take a turn to check.
John: Then we can put the groups in number order.
Our game needs four groups: six, seven, eight and nine pieces. We must sort, count and check before the game begins.
Read aloud. Use large, safe pieces at a reachable table.

textbook_pages.title: Five, then one more

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Count the first five. Touch the next top and say six. Count them all to check.

6
six
Mr Aliyu: After six comes seven. This tray has five on the top row and two on the next row. Count all of them.

7
seven

Adamu: I will move one top each time I say a number.
Try together with six real counters. Then make seven.
Point to each new numeral and say its name.
The last number word tells how many. Spreading a group out does not add tops.

textbook_pages.title: Count eight. Count nine.
textbook_pages.subtitle: Touch each top once. Say how many. Read its numeral.

8
eight

9
nine

John: Give me time to count before you tell me.
Try together: make eight real counters. Spread them out.
Count again. Make nine in another group and check.
Now an adult mixes cards 6, 7, 8, 9. Point to each card and say its number.

textbook_pages.title: Watch the pencil move

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: These are four different numerals. Keep the top of your paper the same way up. Do not turn a 6 over to make a 9.

Start near the top. Curve down and around.
Close the loop at the bottom.

Start at the top left. Draw across to the right.
Slant down to the left.

Start near the top. Make a small loop,
then a lower loop. Join them neatly.

Make the loop at the top first.
Then draw the downstroke on the right.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Compare groups of six and seven. Pair the counters. Seven has one left over, so six comes first. Add eight, then nine: each group has one more.

Before means earlier in counting order. After means later.
Six comes before seven. Nine comes after eight.

Adamu: I put eight before seven.
Grace: Let us count and pair those groups again.
Try together. Put the seven group between six and eight.

Your turn. Write in your exercise book.
Write the number after 6.
Write the number before 9.

Order: 9, 6, 8, 7.

textbook_pages.kicker: For the teacher / Six to nine
textbook_pages.title: Teach, notice and return
textbook_pages.subtitle: Adult guidance / Several short sessions, not a race through four numerals.

elements.text: Sequence. TB1 purpose; TB2-3 quantities six/seven then eight/nine, numeral names and one-to-one counting; TB4 live formation/air-writing; TB5 actual sorting; TB6 modelled quantity order and source tasks; TB7 drawing model, recall/support; TB8 actual sorting/counting/ordering resolution, then fresh checks. Do not advance before each quantity is secure. Existing introductions remain in the opening book.

Prepare. Reachable mats, large safe counters, paper/pencil and cards 1-9. For S002 prepare 6 blue circles, 7 red squares, 8 green triangles and 9 yellow non-square rectangles. Model sorting by outline; shape naming is not assessed. Printed pieces use one colour to show the outline rule. All 30 pieces stay in the same four story groups. Squares remain a special kind of rectangle; use the most specific names here.

Separate skills. Observe quantity, count-once method, recognition, independent naming, dictation/formation and order separately. Counting correctly does not prove reading; copying does not prove writing from dictation. For reversed 6 or 9, keep paper upright and watch the loop/downstroke. Accept usual communication and established adapted writing methods.

Support/recheck. Use counted/uncounted mats and five counters plus one. Model six, then independently check a new seven set. If sorting is hard, sort two small groups then rebuild the target groups. For numeral difficulty, air-write/trace one form, cover it, then dictate it; later retry a different order. Do not label a child as the weak counter.

Delayed recall, next session. Count fresh sets of 6, 7 and 8. Read shuffled cards 9, 6, 8, 7 independently. Dictate nine, seven, six, eight: 9, 7, 6, 8. Order 8, 6, 9: 6, 8, 9. Sort 7 tops and 9 leaves; state each count. Record which skills need support.

textbook_pages.title: Answers and independent checks
textbook_pages.subtitle: Adult task map / TB = this textbook; WB = its paired workbook.

elements.text: Source tasks. P1-04-Q1 (TB6/WB2): 7. Q2 (same): 8. Q3 (same): 6, 7, 8, 9. Q4 (TB7/WB3): exactly 6 separate dots, any clear arrangement. Q5 (same): exactly 9 real objects, each counted once; state 9. Q6 (TB7/WB4): recount 8 once per object; the last word is eight. Moving each counted object is valid. Check the method as well as the total.

Every model. TB2: 6 is five and one; 7 is five and two. TB3: 8 is five and three; 9 is five and four. Spreading changes no quantity. TB4/WB1: recognisable 6, 7, 8, 9; loop below for 6, above for 9. TB5: 6 round/7 square; guided 8 triangle/9 rectangle. TB6: pairing 6 and 7 leaves one unmatched in 7; seven goes between six and eight. Before/after mean earlier/later in counting order. TB7: 2 counters/2 dots; support 6, recheck 7. TB8: groups of 6, 7, 8, 9 in increasing row order.

S002 (TB5/WB5). Mix all 30 pieces. Sort by outline, count and record: 6 circles, 7 squares, 8 triangles, 9 non-square rectangles. Order: 6, 7, 8, 9. Observe actual sorting; written counts alone do not demonstrate it. For story closure (TB8), verify all 30 pieces in these groups before starting the pretend game.

Fresh checks (TB8/WB6). Privately prepare new scattered groups of 8 and 9; answers 8 and 9. S003: count 9 objects once each, then independently name ALL shuffled cards 1-9 without supplied names. Test recognition separately by naming 6, 7, 8, 9 in a different order. Before dictation, cover ALL cards, printed numerals and the pupil's handwritten count answers, including the totals on WB6. S004: dictate eight, six, nine, seven; answers 8, 6, 9, 7, correctly oriented. Do not show answers or read this rubric aloud while testing.
Same tasks on both surfaces count as one check. New physical objects, independently shuffled naming and covered-model dictation are fresh evidence. No tasks have been administered to pupils.

elements.text: Words. Six/seven/eight/nine: quantities after five. Count: say one number word per object. Numeral: written number symbol. Sort: group by a rule. Order: arrange from fewest to most here. Before/after: earlier/later in the counting sequence. Outline: the edge of a shape. Shape names may be read by an adult; they are sorting materials, not a new naming test.

Historical mapping. P1-p02-01: sorting/classifying quantities; -02: identify quantities; -03: count/read through 9; -04: write 6-9; -05: quantity order. Original P1-04-Q1-Q6 prompts, answers and order retained. S002 adds actual four-type sorting; S003 adds shuffled reading; S004 adds independent dictation. The historical baseline and suggested pacing do not establish current curriculum alignment.

lessons.title: A bundle of ten
lessons.goal: Make tens and ones, extending to 20.
lessons.look: Amina ties counting sticks into bundles. Why might a bundle be easier to count?
lessons.learn: Ten ones make one ten. A bundle of ten and 3 loose ones make 13. Ones are also called units. Say numbers from 10 to 20 aloud.
lessons.worked: 14 = 1 ten and 4 ones. Two bundles of ten make 20.
lessons.play: Bundle ten paper strips. Show 11, 15, 18 and 20 using bundles and loose strips.
lessons.hint: Use blunt sticks or paper strips. Tie only bundles of exactly ten.

questions.answer: Ten has ten ones; one has one one.

elements.text: Progression. TB1 purpose; TB2 ten ones, bundle/unbundle without changing quantity; TB3 tens on left/ones on right; TB4-5 gradual building/naming of every number 11-20; TB6 live formation/reading; TB7-8 source tasks; TB9 recall/support; TB10 actual packing and fresh checks. Do not rush a ladder page as one lesson. Teach each number with real materials before proceeding.

Prepare. Large paper strips, loose bands, reachable trays/box, pencil/paper and ordinary cards 10-20. Keep 20 strips for the story; use extra demonstration strips or return all story strips before closure. Every tied ten contains exactly 10 visible/countable strips. The band is not one of the counted strips. Open bundles to verify rather than trusting labels or decorative art.

Observe separately. Does the pupil count each one once, make exactly ten, preserve quantity on tying/untying, read shuffled numerals, place digits correctly and explain zero loose ones in 20? One bundle is one ten, not one one. The left digit counts tens, the right counts loose ones. For 10 versus 1, compare actual ten strips with one strip. Accept usual communication and established adapted writing methods.

Help and fresh recheck. Count 9 then one more, recount 10, tie and open. Privately prepare a different set of 11 or 13 strips. Ask for complete tens and loose ones, then a record: 11 gives 1 ten/1 one; 13 gives 1 ten/3 ones. Give no answer before the attempt. For handwriting, model one two-digit numeral, cover all models and prior answers, then dictate a different one on fresh space.

Delayed recall. Next session build 18 (1 ten and 8 ones) and 10 (1 ten and 0 ones). Read shuffled 19, 12, 20, 11. Cover cards and every prior written/printed numeral, then dictate fifteen, twenty, eleven: 15, 20, 11. Record distinct skill results and revisit difficulties.

elements.text: Words. One: a single item here. Ones/units: single items. A ten contains ten ones; the ones place records loose ones. Bundle of ten: exactly ten ones held together. Tens place: the left position in our two-digit numbers; ones place: the right. Zero ones: no loose ones. Eleven to nineteen: one ten and one to nine extra ones. Twenty: two tens.

Historical mapping. P1-p02-06: recognise ten objects as one group. P1-p02-07: tens/ones with activities extending to 20. Stable P1-05-Q1-Q6 prompts, answers and order retained. elements.text: Prepare. Large safe strips, bands, reachable trays, three boxes, cards 1-99, paper and pencils. A bundle is ten separate strips. Open and recount it. The binding is not counted. Artwork is decorative; exact mathematics uses vector diagrams or actual strips.

Progression. Prior 1-20 check first. Re-teach any gaps before larger numbers. Use several sessions for 21-25, then 26-29, then each decade through 99. For EVERY number in a band, model build/name/formation, build/read/write together, then independent samples. Do not present the band list as one rapid lesson. All numerals use already-taught digits 0-9; demonstrate live formation and spacing again as needed.

Distributed WB checks. Use these band lists in order. Read cards: 25/21/24;29/26/28;39/30/38;49/40/48;59/50/58;69/60/68;79/70/78;89/80/88;99/90/98. Recognise the middle card among:21/22/25;26/27/29;30/31/39;40/41/49;50/51/59;60/61/69;70/71/79;80/81/89;90/91/99. Dictation lists and build/count answers follow on the next page. Cover ALL cards, models and earlier handwriting before dictation. Use fresh space or extra paper. Record count/build/read/recognition/copy/memory-writing separately. Read-aloud cards are visual stimuli, so remain visible only during reading/recognition.

Prior check. Count 7; build 12 and 20; read 5,19,2,10,16; recognise spoken 19 among 12,19,20; after copying 12 cover it and dictate fifteen (15). These are prerequisite samples, not complete 1-20 mastery. Later rotate all earlier values 1-20 across oral counting, mixed reading and covered writing.
Access. Speaking, pointing or moving strips can show understanding. An adult may scribe explanations. Record assisted handwriting separately; do not mistake a motor difficulty for a number error.

Models/guided. 14=one ten/four ones; twenty=two tens/no ones. For every two-digit model, count the bundles to check the tens digit and count the loose strips to check the ones digit. Read the printed whole name. Nine loose ones plus one makes ten loose ones; exchanging makes one more ten and zero loose ones. At transitions 29/39/49/59/69/79/89 become 30/40/50/60/70/80/90. Sequence model 29; guided gaps 50,51; 72 is 7 tens/2 ones; 84 is 8 tens/4 ones; range 62,63,64,65.

Every band WB. Build/count totals respectively: 22/23, 27/28, 31/32, 41/42, 51/52, 61/62, 71/72, 81/82, 91/92. Accept clear bundles of ten and remaining ones. Read cards in each stated order with the correct whole names. Recognition targets:22,27,31,41,51,61,71,81,91. Dictation answers: 24,25; 28,29; 33,39; 43,49; 53,59; 63,69; 73,79; 83,89; 93,99. Copied numbers must match each model; memory trials must be covered.

Names/recall/story. Teen/tens pairs have one ten plus the stated loose ones versus 3-9 tens/no ones; fourteen/forty, fifteen/fifty, sixteen/sixty, seventeen/seventy, eighteen/eighty, nineteen/ninety. For any chosen number21-99, bundles and loose ones must total that number and its whole name must be correct. Recall: count/check ten, tie, retain same total. Ending labels 46,81,93 match 4t6o,8t1o,9t3o and spoken names; actually attach after checking.

elements.text: Fresh checks. Count a prepared 47-strip set (4 checked tens,7 loose). Build spoken thirty-six and eighty-two (3t6o;8t2o). Read shuffled 24,39,40,57,68,70,86,99 aloud: twenty-four, thirty-nine, forty, fifty-seven, sixty-eight, seventy, eighty-six, ninety-nine. Recognise spoken fifty-three among cards 35,53,50. Hide ALL cards, printed models and earlier handwriting; dictate twenty-three, thirty-eight, forty, fifty-six, sixty-seven, seventy-one, eighty-five, ninety-nine: 23,38,40,56,67,71,85,99. Use extra paper; split into brief sessions.

Misconceptions and intervention. A bundle mistaken for one: open and count ten. Reversed digits: build 24, touch two tens/four ones, record places. Teen/tens confusion: contrast 13 and 30 physically; stress whole name. After 29, child says 210: tie the ten loose ones; record 3 tens/0 ones. Zero ignored: compare 60 with 6 physically. Repeat with support, then privately recheck NEW 34 (3t4o), 50 (5t0o), read 17/70, dictate thirty-two (32) after covering. Do not award independent success for the coached example.

Delayed recall next session. Build 58 (5t8o); count prepared 64 (6t4o); read shuffled 31,49,50,62,79,80,95: thirty-one, forty-nine, fifty, sixty-two, seventy-nine, eighty, ninety-five. Recognise ninety-two among 29,92,90. Cover all models/earlier writing; dictate 29,30,44,59,60,78,90,96 using spoken names. Continue new samples in every band and 1-20 in later weeks. A small sample never establishes full-range mastery.

Record. Note independent/assisted/not yet for each mode, date and response. Copying alone does not establish memory writing; pointing alone does not establish naming. No pupil outcomes have been claimed.

elements.text: Words. Digit: one written symbol 0-9. Numeral: written number. Ten: a group of ten ones. Ones: single items; ones place records loose ones. Tens place: left place in these two-digit numerals. Zero: no loose ones in 30,40,...,90. Sequence: numbers in an order. Bundle: tied ten, checked by opening and counting.

Curriculum map. Historical 2012 baseline P1-p03-01 identify/read numbers 1-99: prior check, each band, name contrasts, mixed fresh/delayed cards. P1-p03-02 write numerals 1-99: live formation/copying per band, covered distributed/fresh/delayed dictation; Q1/Q5. Q2 samples reading; Q3/Q4/Q6 consolidate sequence/place value. docs/PRIMARY-1-TEACHING-MAP.md and research/PRIMARY-1-ASSUMPTIONS.json provide baseline/limitations. Term 2 weeks 1-3 is editorial pacing.

elements.text:
Equal parts.
Fair shares.

Aishatu: My box-toy display needs one paper mat. Each of us wants the same space for a drawing. I want to start now!
Mrs Binta: First let us learn to share the whole mat fairly.
Adamu: Nobody should be left out.
Grace: I will check the edges neatly.
John: Let me try a fold before you tell me.
We will make and recognise equal halves and quarters. Keep paper on a reachable table. Use scrap paper instead of food.

textbook_pages.kicker: Chapter seven / Equal halves and quarters
textbook_pages.title: Watch the paper fold
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Say, point or use your workbook or exercise book.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: This complete sheet is one whole. Watch me bring one short edge exactly onto the other. Press the fold. Open the sheet.
The line shows the fold. The two pieces cover the same amount of paper. Fold again to check that they fit exactly on each other. Equal means the same amount of space here.
Each part is a half of the whole. Two equal halves make the whole. I shade one part on my paper: one half is shaded.
Try together. Take a rectangle of scrap paper. Match its short edges, fold and open. Touch each half. Say, "Two equal parts." Turn the sheet. Is each part still a half?
Grace: Turning the sheet changes its direction. It does not change the amount of paper in each half. Keep your folded sheet for the next turn.

textbook_pages.kicker: Chapter seven / Equal halves and quarters
textbook_pages.title: Fold again for quarters
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Say, point or use your workbook or exercise book.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Watch with a square sheet. Match opposite edges and fold in half. Keep it folded. Match the other pair of edges and fold once more. Open all the folds.
There are four equal parts. Each part is a quarter of the whole. Four equal quarters make the whole. I shade just one part: one quarter is shaded.
Try together. Fold your own square in half, then fold it in half again the other way. Open it. Touch and count the four equal parts. Shade one part on your paper.
Adamu: I count four parts. Mrs Binta: Check the amount too. Fold them onto each other: they must fit. Four pieces alone do not prove that they are quarters.

elements.text:
Aishatu: I drew a quick line. Two pieces must be halves!
Mrs Binta: Check them. One has less paper. Two unequal pieces are not halves.
John: The right whole has two equal parts. Each is a half. Aishatu tries again and matches the edges before pressing the fold.
A new way: I draw a line from one corner of a square to the opposite corner. The two triangles fit exactly on each other when folded. Each triangle is a half.
Try together. On paper, copy the square and corner-to-corner line. Point to a half. Explain how the pieces match. Workbook: Check the parts.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Watch me turn a square without changing its pieces. In the tilted square, four equal triangles meet in the middle. One shaded triangle is a quarter.
The paper orange model also has two equal parts. One part is a half. It is paper, not food. Fold a round paper model through its centre to check the matching halves.
Say together: a half is one of two equal parts; a quarter is one of four equal parts. Shape and direction may change. Equal amounts still matter.
Mrs Binta: Now we can read short names. 1/2 is read "one half": one of two equal parts. 1/4 is read "one quarter": one of four equal parts. Say the words as I point. You may answer in words.

Watch me draw a square. I draw one line through the middle from top to bottom, then another from side to side. I count four equal parts. I shade just one.

elements.text: Source questions (textbook p7; workbook pp2-3). Q1: 2 equal parts. Q2: 4 equal parts. Q3: rectangle divided into two equal-area parts; middle vertical/horizontal or corner-to-corner diagonal accepted. Q4: square with four equal-area parts, exactly one shaded; grid or four centre-meeting triangles accepted. Q5: No; unequal amounts are not halves. Q6: whole has four equal parts and exactly one is shaded. Accept equivalent spoken wording.

Models and guided turns (textbook pp2-6; workbook p1). HALF: two matching equal parts, unchanged when turned. QUARTER: four matching parts after perpendicular folds, one shaded. COMPARE: left .3/.7 unequal, right .5/.5 halves. DIAGONAL: two equal triangles each half. ROTATED: four equal triangles, one shaded quarter. FRUIT: two equal parts, one shaded half. NOTATION: 1/2 one half; 1/4 one quarter. DRAW: rectangle middle line; square middle cross with one part shaded. Workbook p1: top-left half, top-right quarter; bottom-left no, bottom-right yes. Require amount as well as count.

Support, recheck and extension (textbook p8; workbook p4). Helped rectangle: two equal halves. New tall rectangle: one middle line makes equal halves; new square: four equal parts, one indicated quarter. A different half may be horizontal, vertical or diagonal. Test equal area by folding/overlay, not matching shape alone; different-shaped pieces can also have equal area. Adults may verify other mathematically valid partitions.

textbook_pages.kicker: For the teacher / Equal halves and quarters
textbook_pages.title: Story, fresh checks and delayed recall
textbook_pages.subtitle: Adult reference / Read with both exact chapter books.

elements.text: Story (textbook p9; workbook p5). One square whole, four equal quarters, one drawing per friend. Four quarters exhaust the whole with no overlap. Names on textbook mat: Aishatu upper-left, Adamu upper-right, Grace lower-left, John lower-right. Workbook may place names or drawings in any order. Require one equal share for each, no excluded friend.

Fresh tasks (textbook p10; workbook p6). Left: half, two equal parts, one shaded despite rotation. Middle paper fruit: quarter, four equal parts, one shaded. Right: neither, two unequal parts (.3/.7); shading alone does not name a fraction. New drawing: four equal-area parts of a whole with exactly one shaded. Recall: half one of two equal parts; quarter one of four equal parts.

Intervene, then new recheck. If counting alone: overlap unequal paper pieces to show unequal space. Match folded edges before naming halves. If all shaded parts called quarters: compare equal two-part and equal four-part wholes, touching each part. If rotation confuses: turn the same sheet slowly. After help, give a NEW wide rectangle for halves and NEW square for quarters. Do not score coached work as independent.

Delayed recall next session. With blank paper and no models, ask the pupil to make equal halves of a new rectangle and quarters of a new square, point to one part of each and explain. Present a square split diagonally and a paper orange split into unequal pieces: half; not halves. Check again in later weeks with different orientations. Record assistance.

textbook_pages.title: Words, evidence and next steps

elements.text: Glossary. Whole: the complete object or shape being shared. Equal parts: parts with the same amount of area (space inside the shape). Half: one of two equal parts of a whole. Quarter: one of four equal parts. Fold: bend paper so parts lie on each other. Unequal: different amounts. Symbols 1/2 and 1/4 are read only after concrete models; symbol writing is not required here.

elements.text: Textbook (TB) and workbook (WB) page links refer to this chapter pair. All original tasks retain their prompt/answer meanings. Oral, pointing or practical demonstrations are valid; accept any clear dot arrangement.

TB2: JOIN-MODEL 2+1=3; the same three tops move. JOIN-GUIDED 1+1=2.
TB3: SIGNS-MODEL 2+1=3 and 3=2+1; both sides have value 3. SIGNS-GUIDED 1+2=3.
TB4: THREE-MODEL 1+1+2=4; 2+2+2=6. THREE-GUIDED 1+1+1=3.
TB5 / WB1: DRAW-MODEL 1+1=2; 2 books+1=3 books. DRAW-GUIDED draw 1 then 2 dots, total 3. WB-GUIDED first 2; then 3 dots, total 3.

TB6 / WB2-3 originals: Q1 1+2=3; Q2 2+2=4; Q3 1+1+1=3. Q4 two dots and one more, total 3. Q5 one dot and three more, total 4 books. Q6 draw 1+2 and 2+1; both total 3. Accept rearranged drawings with the correct counts and explanation.
TB7 / WB4-5: RECALL plus joins amounts; equals means same value; touch/count each once. HELP 1+1=2. RECHECK 2+1=3. SWAP both orders total 3 because no counter is added or removed.

TB8 / WB5-6: STORY 2+1=3 tops; all four take turns (not a top each). FRESH-TWO 1+3=4. FRESH-THREE 1+2+2=5. FRESH-EQUALS each side has value 4 or 5 respectively. Accept speech plus matching objects instead of fluent writing.

elements.text: Suggested sessions: TB1-2 concrete joining; TB3 signs and equality; TB4 three sets; TB5 drawing; TB6 / WB2-3 independent tasks; TB7 help; TB8 and WB6 fresh checks. This is flexible editorial pacing, not an official timetable.

Read directions aloud. Use large safe counters or paper circles. Keep all materials reachable for seated participation. Allow touch, pointing, speech and drawing. Model the move into one row; do not introduce counting-on, carrying or totals through eighteen here.

Observe: Does the child preserve all objects, count each once, distinguish the separate sets from the total and read the entire number sentence? If a child counts a set twice, return to 1+1, moving each counter once into one row. Then use the new 2+1 recheck (TB7 / WB4). If equals is treated as an answer arrow, build 3 and 2+1 side by side and read 3=2+1.

Delayed recall, next session: Without showing earlier answers, ask the child to join two and two counters and record the total. Then join one, one and two. Ask whether 4=2+2 is true and why. Answers: 4; 4; yes, both sides have value 4. Record whether the child worked independently or with support.
Do not infer mastery from copied numerals. Return to concrete objects when needed.

elements.text: Page numbers here are PDF ordinals for adults; pupil links use printed titles. Any clear correct dot arrangement, oral explanation or practical demonstration is valid. Count-on words must begin AFTER the held number.

TB2 / WB1: COUNT-MODEL 4+2=6 (5,6); count all 6. COUNT-GUIDED 2+3=5 (3,4,5); all 5.
TB3 / WB1: THREE-SMALL-MODEL 3+2=5, then 5+4=9. THREE-SMALL-GUIDED 1+2+3=6; first 3, then 6. Each amount once.
TB4: ZERO-MODEL 6+0=6 and0+3=3; ZERO-GUIDED 5+0=5. Move nothing for zero.
TB5: CROSS-MODEL 8+5=13 (9..13); CROSS-GUIDED 7+4=11 (8..11). Count-all checks 13 and 11.

TB6 / TB9 / WB5: THREE-LARGE-MODEL 4+5+6=15: hold 4, count 5..9, then 10..15. THREE-LARGE-GUIDED 9+0+8=17: still 9, then 10..17. S005 exact answers 15 and 17, all three addends once; correct count-on or count-all demonstration.
TB7 / WB4: CHECK-MODEL 8+6=14, six new count words 9..14; incorrect 13 repeats starting 8. Count all 14. CHECK-GUIDED 5+2=7 (6,7); wrong 6 is one too few.
TB8 / WB2-4 originals: Q1=7; Q2=6; Q3=8 (first 5, then 8); Q4=18; Q5=12 seeds; Q6 count all 14 objects OR count on six from 8 (9..14). Both are valid; comparing both methods strengthens checking.

textbook_pages.kicker: Chapter nine / Count on to add
textbook_pages.title: Support, fresh checks and recall
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text:
TB10 / WB6-7: RECALL first new word is the next number after held start; zero adds none; count-all checks. HELP 2+1=3 (say 3); RECHECK 3+2=5 (4,5), then count all 5.
TB11 / WB7: STORY 8+5=13, count 9..13; all 13 original counters conserved. The printed pictures are a model of the same inventory, not extra counters.

TB12 / WB8: FRESH-TWO 5+7=12 (6..12); FRESH-THREE 2+0+9=11 (still 2, then 3..11); FRESH-CHECK 6+3=9, claim 8 is false;7,8,9 and all 9. Equals means same value on both sides. Accept counters, dots and oral explanations, with accurate totals.

Suggested teaching: distribute TB2-7 over short sessions with movement and turns. If the held number is counted again, use TB10 two-plus-one intervention and different three-plus-two recheck. If a third set is missed, keep it separate until its turn. For zero, point to an empty space and move no object. Do not introduce column addition or counting beyond 18 here.

DELAYED next session: Cover earlier answers. Privately give six counters and five more: 11. Then three, zero and seven: 10. Ask whether 7+2=8 is true: no, correct 9. Ask the child to count on and then check all. Record independence/support. Read aloud and accept pointing, speech or seated action.

elements.text: Glossary: count on: keep a known amount and say the next numbers for added objects. Sum/total: how many altogether. Addend (adult term): an amount being added. Zero: no objects in the set. Check: use a method to see whether a result is right. Equals (=): has the same value as.

Historical mapping: P1-p04-02 two/three addends below 10; P1-p04-03 two/three totals through 18 under the documented inclusive provisional bound; P1-p04-05 checking accuracy. S005 retained exactly. elements.text: Adult record: PDF page ordinals below; stable IDs are not pupil numbering. Accept correct drawings in any arrangement, spoken explanations or practical demonstrations. A bundle must contain ten ones. Count each strip once in an all-ones check.

TB2 PLACE: 12 is 1 ten and 2 ones; guided 14 is 1 ten and 4 ones.
TB3 JOIN-MODEL / TB4 COLUMN-MODEL: 12+15=27; 2+5=7 ones, 1+1=2 tens; untie/count all 27.
TB4 / WB1 GUIDED: 11+12=23; 1+2=3 ones, 1+1=2 tens; check all 23.
TB5 LARGE-MODEL: 23+14=37; 3+4=7 ones, 2+1=3 tens; check all 37.

TB6 ZERO-MODEL: 30+10=40; zero ones and four tens; count 40 unbundled strips. ZERO-GUIDED: 20+13=33; 3 ones, 3 tens.
TB7 ONE-DIGIT-MODEL / WB3 Q4: 14+5=19; 5 under 4 in ones; 9 ones, 1 ten; count 19.
TB8 CHECK-MODEL: 12+11=23, not 24. TB8 / WB5 CHECK-GUIDED: 13+12=25, not 24. Rebuild/join/count all to check.

TB9 / WB2-4 source questions: Q1 25; Q2 37; Q3 40; Q4 19; Q5 33 pencils; Q6 two tens plus one ten and three ones make three tens and three ones. These retain all six original prompts and answer meanings.

textbook_pages.kicker: Chapter ten / Add tens and ones
textbook_pages.title: Support, checks and delayed recall
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text:
TB10 / WB6: RECALL tens under tens, ones under ones; add ones then tens; check by joining and counting all unbundled strips. HELP 10+2=12; RECHECK 10+4=14. Use a different fresh recheck after any extra demonstration.
TB11 STORY / WB4 Q5: 22+11=33 pencils; three tens and three ones. Original stock is conserved; practice strips are separate.

TB12 / WB7 fresh: FRESH-TWO 24+13=37 (7 ones,3 tens). FRESH-ZERO 20+20=40 (0 ones,4 tens). FRESH-CHECK 12+5=17, not 62; align the 5 under the 2 as ones, not under the 1 as tens. EXPLAIN: ones totals 7,0,7 are below ten, so no new bundle. Independent all-ones checks give 37,40,17.

Suggested sessions and misconceptions: teach TB2-4, then TB5-7, then TB8-12 in several short sessions. Give all four children turns. If 5 is placed in tens, physically put five loose strips in ones. If 40 becomes 4, contrast four loose strips with four actual bundles. If needed return to TB10, then its fresh 10+4 recheck.

DELAYED next session: Cover all earlier printed and handwritten answers. Give 13+16 (29), 20+10 (30), then the claim 21+7=91 (false:28). Ask for aligned recording and a build/join/count-all check. Record independence and support.

elements.text: Glossary: ten: a group of ten ones. One: a single item. Place: a digit's position in a number. Total/sum: how many altogether. Add (+): join amounts. Equals (=): has the same value as. Check: use a method to see whether an answer is right.

elements.text: Adult record: TB/WB refer to PDF page ordinals. Stable IDs are adult references. Accept correct spoken, pointed, practical or drawn responses. Add remaining and removed quantities to recover the start. Crossed dots remain visible but are not counted as remaining.

TB2 SMALL-MODEL: 7−3=4; 4+3=7. TB3 SMALL-GUIDED: 6−2=4; 4+2=6. ALL-MODEL: 4−4=0; 0+4=4. TB4 BACK-MODEL: 8−3=5; first step is 7, then 6,5; 5+3=8.
TB5 CROSS-MODEL: 14−6=8; remove 4 to reach 10, then 2 to reach 8; 8+6=14.
TB6/WB1 CROSS-GUIDED: 12−5=7; steps 11,10,9,8,7. 8+5=13 fails; 7+5=12.
TB7 CHECK-MODEL: 9−4=5; 5+4=9.
WB1 CROSSOUT-MODEL: 4−1=3; 3+1=4; one crossed dot is removed, three uncrossed remain.

TB8 / WB2 Q1: original 7−2: 5; check 5+2=7.
TB8 / WB2 Q2: original 9−9: 0; check 0+9=9.
TB8 / WB3 Q3: original 15−4: 11; check 11+4=15.
TB8 / WB3 Q4: original 18−9: 9; check 9+9=18.
TB8 / WB4 Q5: 12 chalk pieces, use 3: 9 pieces remain; 9+3=12. Used pieces stay visible.
TB8 / WB4 Q6: addition check for 13−5=8 is 8+5=13. Eight remaining plus five removed restore thirteen.

elements.text:
TB9/WB5 RECALL: take away; first backward step follows the start; remaining + removed = start. SMALL-HELP 3−1=2, 2+1=3. SMALL-RECHECK 5−2=3, 3+2=5. TB10/WB5 CROSS-HELP: 11−2=9, 9+2=11. CROSS-RECHECK 11−3=8, 8+3=11.
TB11 STORY: 12−3=9 pieces on mat; 3 on tray; 9+3=12.

Teach in short sessions: TB2-4 within nine, TB5-6 crossing ten, TB7-12 checking and independence. If pupils count the start as a backward step, move one counter first, then say the number left. If they count removed counters, use separate labelled spaces. Empty the remaining space to teach zero. Never hide or discard removed objects.
DELAYED next session: Cover all answers. Independently solve 7−4=3 and 16−8=8; check 13−4=9 by 9+4=13. Ask for practical checks (3+4=7, 8+8=16). Record support and independence.

elements.text: Glossary: subtract (−): take away an amount. Remain/left: still there after taking away. Zero (0): none. Check: see if an answer is right. Add (+): join amounts. Equals (=): has the same value. Backwards: move towards smaller numbers, one step for each object removed.

Some fresh-check numbers vary so pupils transfer the method to examples not already taught. Original Q1-Q6 are retained. S007 belongs to the next unit and is unchanged. elements.text:
Find the missing part.
Check both sides.

Mr Aliyu: Aishatu needs 7 tops for her box-toy school. There are 3 on the mat. The rest are inside a bag we cannot see through. How many are hidden?
Aishatu: I want to open it! I will wait while we work it out.
John: Let me solve the secret before you tell me.
Grace: I will keep the groups tidy.
Adamu: Everyone gets a turn. Put the bag where we can all reach it.
We will find missing numbers and check our answers.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu joins 2 counters and 3 counters. He counts 5 altogether. The sign = means both sides have the same amount.
One part
Other part

2 + 3 = 5
5 = 2 + 3
Read either way: the amounts are equal.
In 2 + __ = 5, the blank holds a number. Replace the blank with 3: 2 + 3 = 5. An answer-writing line is only a place to write your reply. It is not another missing number.

textbook_pages.title: Teaching across short sessions
textbook_pages.subtitle: Adult guidance / Read pupil prompts aloud.

elements.text: Teach one new missing-number position at a time. Revisit addition and subtraction with counters before this chapter. Read all prompts aloud. Introduce - as take away and + as join; = means equal amounts. A blank represents a number, not an instruction to calculate everything on its left.

Suggested sequence: equality and addition; removed and starting amounts; reversed equality and substitution; related families; everyday checking; independent practice; targeted help and recheck; story ending and fresh checks. Take additional short sessions when needed. This is editorial pacing, not an official scheme.

Textbook/workbook page pairs: 12/1, 13/2, 14/3, 15/4, 16/5; help 17/6 through 22/11; fresh checks 24/12, 25/13, 26/14. Workbook page labels are printed above each title. Textbook users can use counters and an ordinary exercise book for every response. Do not mark the textbook.

Keep counters large and reachable. Accept speech, pointing, moving objects or drawing as evidence before writing. Never tell John an answer before his turn. Rotate the helper and speaker. Count hidden story tops only after opening; the artwork does not encode their number.

textbook_pages.title: Notice, help and check later
textbook_pages.subtitle: Adult guidance / Read pupil prompts aloud.

elements.text: Look for: adding the visible numbers regardless of blank position; treating = as an answer arrow; giving the removed amount when the start is unknown; guessing without substitution; counting a counter twice. Ask the pupil to name whole, known part and missing part before moving objects.

Support: choose the matching smaller-step page. Model with counters and allow the pupil to copy the action. Close that example, put those counters away and use the new recheck. Record success by objective, not by a total score. Re-teach if the recheck is unsuccessful.

Fresh check: use the last three pupil practice pages without help. All six objectives have separate fresh evidence. At a later session, use the six prompts in the complete answer map marked delayed. Keep the book closed and use new objects. Record prompt, response, method and any help.

Story preparation: place exactly 4 tops in an opaque bag and 3 on the mat before the opening. Tell the whole 7 without displaying the hidden set. Do not reveal the 4 until the story ending. All independent tasks use separate sets; they do not alter the story stock.

P1-12-EQUAL-MODEL / model
The blank names one missing number. Equal means the same amount on both sides.
Answer: 2 + 3 = 5 and 5 = 2 + 3 describe equal amounts. Blank in 2 + __ = 5 is 3.

P1-12-ADD-LAST-MODEL / model
Mr Aliyu: Find 1 + __ = 4. Put out 1 counter. Count on: 2, 3, 4. We added 3 counters. Replace the blank: 1 + 3 = 4. Both sides make 4.
Answer: 3; substitute 1+3=4.

Answer: 4; 4+2=6.

Answer: 2; 2+4=6.

elements.text: Blank: a place for one missing number. Part: some of a whole. Whole: all the parts together. Equal: the same amount. Substitute: replace the blank with a number and check the original sentence. Related: sentences using the same whole and its two parts.

Historical objective mapping: P1-p06-01 missing addition; P1-p06-02 everyday addition checks; P1-p06-03 missing subtraction; P1-p06-04 everyday subtraction checks; P1-p07-01 open statements; P1-p07-02 related open statements. All six have models, guided and independent work, help, a new recheck, fresh checks and delayed checks.

Drafted from the documented historical 2012 baseline and provisional production assumptions. Current NERDC and Gombe alignment and adoption are unverified. Local educator review, pupil and accessibility trials, physical print tests and printer approval remain pending. This chapter pair is an extract, not the complete annual book.

lessons.title: Pretend coins and change
lessons.goal: Identify coin values and calculate with pretend kobo.
lessons.look: Daniel makes paper tokens for a pretend shop. Why does a value label matter?
lessons.learn: Nigerian money is called naira and kobo. 100 kobo = 1 naira. Use labelled pretend tokens: 1k, 5k, 10k and 25k. These are historical-value exercises, not real prices or a claim about money circulating today.
lessons.worked: 5k + 10k = 15k. Pay 10k for a pretend 6k item: change is 10k − 6k = 4k.
lessons.play: Draw token outlines and label values. An adult may show a genuine coin for identification and supervised pencil tracing. Never mark or alter real money.
lessons.hint: Use large paper tokens. Real prices and currently used denominations differ.

questions.prompt: Why read a token value, not just count tokens?
questions.answer: Different tokens can have different values.

source_tasks.source_prompt: Why read a token value, not just count tokens?
source_tasks.source_answer: Different tokens can have different values.

supplementary_source_tasks.source_prompt: Using the teacher's verified genuine Nigerian coin examples or verified official images, point to each coin and say its denomination. Distinguish coins from the book's pretend tokens.
supplementary_source_tasks.source_answer: Each value agrees with the teacher's dated verified denomination checklist; do not infer value from size or token count.

supplementary_source_tasks.source_prompt: With supervision, place an available genuine coin under brown paper and white paper in turn and make a gentle pencil rubbing on each sheet. Say which coin was used.
supplementary_source_tasks.source_answer: Two recognisable surface rubbings made by tracing the coin through the paper; coin and paper intact; stated value matches the example.

textbook_pages.title: Our pretend shop
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text:
Read the value.
Find the change.

Mrs Binta: Our box-toy shop has one pretend map ticket. It costs 6k. We have a 10k payment. How much must the shop give back?
Aishatu: I built the shop. I will wait for a fair turn.
Adamu: Everyone can join our shop story.
Grace: I will keep the value cards neat.
John: Put them within reach. Let me solve the change puzzle.
We will read money values, make totals, find change and try real-coin rubbings when materials are ready.

textbook_pages.title: Value is not a card count
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: These rectangles are pretend value cards, not pictures of real coins. Our old-value shop is a game. These are not today's prices. Nigerian money uses naira and kobo. 100 kobo = 1 naira. We write k for kobo.
Mrs Binta: Read the label. This card has value 10k.
Two cards can have the same total value as one card.
5k + 5k = 10k. Value tells how much; card count tells how many cards. Grace reads each label before adding. The sign = means equal value.
To draw a pretend token: draw a rectangle like the one above, then write 10k inside. This completed card is your model. Daniel is a fictional story-card name.

textbook_pages.title: Meet genuine coins
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Adult: prepare at least two DIFFERENT verified Nigerian coin denominations, as genuine coins or dated verified official images, and a written value checklist. Record the verification source, date and values. Use only examples you can verify. Without them, skip this activity and record not assessed. Pretend cards cannot replace real examples.

Mrs Binta shows: This is a genuine coin or a verified picture of one. I check its denomination: that means its money value. I point to it and say its value from our checklist. I do not guess from its size.
Try together. Adamu points to an example. Say its value with Mrs Binta. Grace matches it to the adult's value label. Compare it with our rectangular pretend cards. Which is the real example?
Then try on your own on workbook page 1, or point and speak using the adult's real examples beside your exercise book. The adult records what you say.

textbook_pages.title: A coin surface on paper
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Adult: provide a verified genuine coin, pencil, brown paper and white paper. Work at a reachable table. Keep the coin under paper. Rub gently with the pencil side on the paper only; never mark the coin. Keep coin and paper intact. Supervise small objects. Without all materials, record not assessed.

Watch Mrs Binta. She says the verified coin's value. She places it under brown paper and holds the paper still. She gently moves the pencil side across the paper. The surface pattern appears. She repeats with white paper.

Try together. Aishatu holds her paper still while the adult checks the coin underneath. Grace tries again if the first rubbing smudges. Make a rubbing on each colour of paper. Tell the adult which coin you used.
Use workbook page 2 or separate brown and white sheets kept with your exercise book. An adult may secure the brown sheet to the workbook. A drawn outline is not a surface rubbing.

textbook_pages.title: Join the values
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: A total is the value altogether. Read 10k and 5k. Start at 10 and count on 5: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. 10k + 5k = 15k.
Try together. John reads these labels. Adamu says, "Three cards means 3k." John asks him to add the values. Count on from 5. What is the total?
Say the total, then write the addition in your exercise book. Now work alone on textbook page 7. Respond on workbook page 3 or in your exercise book.

textbook_pages.title: Count on for change
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Cost means the amount asked for. Payment is the amount given. Change is the amount given back. Our ticket costs 6k. Pay 10k. Count from the cost up to the payment: 7, 8, 9, 10. Four counts: change is 4k.

10k - 6k = 4k.
Check: 6k + 4k = 10k.
Cost plus change equals payment.
Try together. Grace buys a pretend label costing 5k. She pays 8k. Aishatu counts on from 5 to 8. How much change? Check by adding cost and change.

Use labelled paper cards or count with your fingers. Say the change and check aloud; write in your exercise book. Then try textbook page 8 on your own. Respond on workbook page 4 or in your exercise book.

Why read a token value, not just count tokens? Say your reason or write it on workbook page 5 OR in your ordinary exercise book.

textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Close the model pages. Tell a partner what you remember. Try before you ask for help.

How is a real coin different from a pretend value card?

How do you find the total of cards?

How do you find and check change?

What must be under the paper for a real rubbing?
Point, speak or show with materials. Do not write in this textbook. Use your exercise book if you want to draw your thinking. Next use the help you need, then try its new check.

textbook_pages.title: Help with real values
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Use two verified real examples with DIFFERENT values. Mrs Binta says one value. Match it by pointing. Look at each example with her, not at its size.

Now try a new check.
The adult now reverses the two examples and removes the value labels. Name each value yourself.
Say your answer or use your exercise book. For genuine coin work the adult records the result; absent resources mean not assessed. This is a new check after help, not the fresh independent check.

textbook_pages.title: Help with rubbing
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Hold one genuine coin under white paper. The adult steadies it and shows a short gentle pencil stroke. Repeat with brown paper.

Now try a new check.
With fresh brown and white paper, place the coin yourself and make both rubbings under supervision. Say its verified value.
Say your answer or use your exercise book. For genuine coin work the adult records the result; absent resources mean not assessed. This is a new check after help, not the fresh independent check.

textbook_pages.title: Help with totals
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Read two 1k labels. Join their values: 1k + 1k = 2k. Touch each label once.

Now try a new check.
Read cards labelled 5k and 1k. Find their total without help.
Say your answer or write in your exercise book. This is a new check after help. Try it before the fresh independent check.

textbook_pages.title: Help with change
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text: Pay 5k for a 3k item. Count on: 4, 5. Two counts: 2k change. Check 3k + 2k = 5k.

Now try a new check.
A pretend item costs 4k. Pay 6k. Find the change without help. Check your answer.
Say your answer or write in your exercise book. This is a new check after help. Try it before the fresh independent check.

textbook_pages.title: The ticket is ready
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.

elements.text:
John: The ticket costs 6k. I pay 10k. I worked out 4k change.
Grace: I give back 4k and keep 6k for the shop.

elements.text: Four historical objectives. Recognise genuine denominations; combine values through 25k; find change from payments through 10k; rub genuine coin surfaces through brown and white paper. Pretend arithmetic does not establish genuine-coin identification. All real-resource stages are conditional opportunities, not recorded pupil outcomes.

Adult: prepare at least two DIFFERENT verified Nigerian coin denominations, as genuine coins or dated verified official images, and a written value checklist. Record the verification source, date and values. Use only examples you can verify. Without them, skip this activity and record not assessed. Pretend cards cannot replace real examples.

Adult: provide a verified genuine coin, pencil, brown paper and white paper. Work at a reachable table. Keep the coin under paper. Rub gently with the pencil side on the paper only; never mark the coin. Keep coin and paper intact. Supervise small objects. Without all materials, record not assessed.

Observation rubric: record date, exact resources/checklist, each response and assistance. Recognition: every value agrees and real examples are distinguished from pretend cards. Rubbing: two recognisable surface patterns through the specified papers; correct verified value; intact materials. Record independent / supported / needs another try / not assessed. elements.text: Routes and sequence. Textbook 1 story/goal; 2 values; 3 genuine model/guided to workbook 1; 4 rubbing to workbook 2; 5 totals; 6 change; 7-9 independent originals to workbook 3-5; 10 recall BEFORE help; 11-14 help and new rechecks; 15 closure; 16 fresh to workbook 6-7. Every printed independent prompt and value is local in both artifacts. Respond in the exact workbook page OR an ordinary exercise book; genuine activities use verified materials and separate sheets. No textbook marking.

Misconceptions and support. Three cards do not mean 3k: read and add labels (page 13). Change is not the cost: count from cost up to payment and add to check (page 14). A copied outline is not rubbing (page 12). Size does not prove denomination (page 11). Keep genuine-resource outcomes separate from pretend arithmetic. Permit pointing, speech, seated handling and an adult scribe; record help honestly.

Current NERDC alignment, adoption, local educator review, pupil/accessibility trials and physical/printer approval remain pending.

lessons.goal: Compare and order lengths and measure with body units.
lessons.look: Zainab compares two strings for a garden bed. Where should their ends start?

lessons.play: Measure a table in your spans and a safe path in your steps. Record whose units you used. A seated child can use a paper strip instead.
lessons.hint: Body units vary. Do not compare different pupils’ counts as if their spans were equal.

elements.text:
Compare lengths.
Measure fairly.

Mr Aliyu: Our box-toy school needs a strip to cover its name label. Which strip will reach?
Aishatu: I built the school. I will wait while we compare.
Adamu: Give everyone a fair turn with the strips.
Grace: I will line up the ends neatly.
John: Put the puzzle within reach. Let me try before you tell me.
We will compare, order and measure lengths to choose a useful strip.

textbook_pages.title: Start together, then compare
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Use the workbook or an exercise book.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Length is how far something reaches from one end to the other. Move the strips so their starts meet. Compare the other ends. Colour and position do not tell length.
A
B
C
D

B is shortest. C comes next. A is longest of A, B and C. A and D reach equally far: they have the same length.
Grace: From shortest to longest: B, C, A. I checked the ends.

Mr Aliyu puts his finger flat on paper. He marks its start and tip. He lifts his finger. He draws a line from the start mark past the tip mark. He puts his finger back: the line reaches beyond it. His line is longer. Watch your teacher do this before you try.

textbook_pages.title: Repeat one unit carefully
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Use the workbook or an exercise book.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Open one hand: thumb tip to little-finger tip is a hand span. Keep that same spread. Mark its end, lift and start there again. Repeat with no gaps or overlaps. Count full spans.
Watch me measure a reachable table. Say whose spans and how many. If a part is left, say the full count and a part. Do not call a part a whole span.
Distance is how far from one place to another. On a clear, safe path, watch me repeat my usual step heel-to-heel. Keep steps as equal as possible. Mark the finish. Count my steps; name my unit.
A paper-strip unit works the same way. Each gap below is one copy of the same strip. A is 3 units; B is 5. The label needs 4. B reaches; A is too short.
A
B
Label
People have different spans and steps. Their counts alone cannot tell which object is longer. Use one person and unit for a fair comparison.

elements.text: Prepare: similar safe paper strips, pencils, book, reachable table, fixed paper-strip unit and label. Adult cuts paper. Clear a short route; supervise steps. No ruler or centimetres are needed. Read aloud; pointing, speech and moving objects are valid responses. Place all materials within reach.

Misconceptions and help: If a pupil chooses by position/colour, align starts and trace to the far ends. If ordering is hard, compare two then add the third. If units gap or overlap, mark each finish and restart there. Different people's counts alone do not show longer: use one person's unit. For leftovers record full units and a part. Recheck with new materials on the try-again page.

Glossary: length: extent end to end; longer/shorter: more/less length; equal length: same reach with starts aligned; distance: how far between places; hand span: thumb-tip to little-finger-tip spread; unit: one chosen repeat; step: one repeated pace; order: arrange by length.

Provisional mapping: historical P1-p09-01 to 05; source Q1-Q6 and S010-S012. Assumptions P1-A03/A09 apply. Current NERDC alignment and adoption are not established.

lessons.title: Our day in order
lessons.goal: Sequence everyday activities and use time words.
lessons.look: The friends describe a school day. What could you do before coming to school?
lessons.learn: Time helps order events. Morning comes before afternoon. Evening comes before night. Routines differ. Use before and after to describe a day.
lessons.worked: In Amina’s story: wake up, wash, eat, then go to school. Eating is before going to school.
lessons.play: Draw three routine cards. A partner puts them in your chosen order. Tell a story using first, next and last.
lessons.hint: Accept varied home routines. No pupil must disclose private home details.

questions.prompt: Which comes first: morning or afternoon?
In Amina’s story, what follows washing?
Explain before with your own two events.
questions.answer: The first event occurs earlier than the second.

textbook_pages.title: A mixed-up story strip
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Listen while an adult reads the cards.

elements.text:
Our day in order
Before and after

Mrs Binta: Our toy-school display needs a story strip. The cards are mixed up!
Aishatu: I made the box toy. I can wait while we sort its story.
Adamu: Give everyone a fair turn.
Grace: Let us keep the cards neat.
John: Put them within reach. Let me solve the order first.
We will put events in order and say when things happen at home and school.

textbook_pages.title: Watch a story in order
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Listen while an adult reads the cards.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Listen to Amina, a child in our pretend story. She wakes, washes, eats, then goes to school. This is her story. Other families may do things differently.

First
Wake

Next
Wash

Then
Eat

Last: go to school.
First starts the story. Next tells what follows. Last ends this story. Before means earlier. After means later.
Eating is after washing. Washing is before eating. Eating is before going to school. Watch me act the cards in that order. You may watch, point or act from your seat.
The order comes from the story, not from where a loose card lies.

textbook_pages.title: Watch completed drawing cards
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Listen while an adult reads the cards.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: I draw a toy-school story. Watch the finished pictures. First I draw a wall. Next I add a roof. Last I add a door. I keep each earlier part.
First: wall
Next: roof
Last: door
I point to each picture: wall first, roof next, door last. Adding the roof comes after the wall and before the door. I can tell this story without writing words.

Aishatu: The pictures show my idea! I will use this method to draw another story later.
An adult can draw or hold cards for you. Your pointing, words or actions can show the order.

textbook_pages.title: Parts of a day
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Listen while an adult reads the cards.

elements.text:
Mrs Binta: We name parts of a day in this order:
morning, afternoon, evening, night.
After night, another morning comes. Days keep going.
Here is my pretend day. Listen to where and when.

Morning
Home: wash

Morning
School: read

Afternoon
Home: make toy

Evening: tell a story at home.
Night: sleep at home.
Reading can also happen at home, in the evening or at another time. Different schools have different routines. No activity belongs to only one day part.
We can use invented routines. You never need to tell private home details.

textbook_pages.title: Try the story together
textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Listen while an adult reads the cards.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: In this story, take paper at school in the morning. Then draw there. Later, show the drawing at home in the afternoon. Point in the story order.

Show drawing
Home: afternoon

Take paper
School: morning

Draw
School: morning

Grace: Show it first because that card is first here?
John: Let us check the story. We need paper before we draw.
Adamu: Everyone may move a card. Tell Grace what happens first, next and last.
Together say when the home activity happens. Say when the school activities happen. Could a different school draw in the afternoon? Yes, if that is its routine.
Your turn: workbook page 1, or say, point, act or draw in an ordinary exercise book. Keep this textbook reusable.

textbook_pages.subtitle: Read together. Listen while an adult reads the cards.

Show picture
School: next morning

Collect leaf
Home: afternoon

textbook_pages.title: Answer map 1
textbook_pages.subtitle: Teacher guidance / provisional chapter extract

elements.text:
P1-15-SEQUENCE-MODEL / model
Amina: wake, wash, eat, school. First wake; wash next; school last; eating follows washing and is before school. These are this fictional story's choices, not a universal routine.

P1-15-DRAW-MODEL / model
Completed drawings: first wall; next wall with roof; last wall with roof and door. Roof is after wall and before door. This is a drawing story, not a required home routine.

P1-15-DAY-MODEL / model
Within the stated day: morning, afternoon, evening, night. In Mrs Binta's story: home wash morning; school reading morning; home toy-making afternoon; home storytelling evening; home sleep night. Reading may also occur at home or other times; next morning follows night.

textbook_pages.title: Answer map 2
textbook_pages.subtitle: Teacher guidance / provisional chapter extract

elements.text:
P1-15-GUIDED / guided
Stated story: first take paper at school in the morning; next draw at school in the morning; last show drawing at home in the afternoon. Drawing follows taking paper and is before showing. Grace's reversal is corrected using the story, not the page position.

P1-15-INDEPENDENT / independent
Stated story: first collect a leaf at home in the afternoon; next draw it at home in the afternoon; last show the picture at school the next morning. Draw is after collect and before show; both contexts and stated parts of day are required. Across-night sequence is explicitly two days.

P1-15-RECALL / recall
Without help, recall first/next/last and before/after; give a coherent story with one home and one school activity, naming plausible day parts. Pointing, speaking or acting is valid; accept fictional routines. Record recall before providing help.

textbook_pages.title: Answer map 3
textbook_pages.subtitle: Teacher guidance / provisional chapter extract

elements.text:
P1-15-HELP / help
With two cards: first open a storybook at home in the evening; next read it at home in the evening. Opening is before reading. Add the third card: close it last, after reading. School example: teacher reads a story in the afternoon in the stated school. Same activity can happen in more than one setting/time.

P1-15-RECHECK / recheck
New recheck without supplied answers: first take clay at school in the afternoon; next shape clay there in the afternoon; last show the toy at home in the evening. Taking is before shaping; showing after shaping. Name school/afternoon and home/evening. Support may read and move cards but cannot supply the response.

P1-15-CLOSURE / story
Aishatu's toy-school picture sequence is wall, roof, door. Put the story strip with it: make toy at home in the afternoon, then share at school next morning. Opening problem resolved by an ordered exhibit; Adamu gives fair reachable turns; all four contribute.

textbook_pages.title: Answer map 4
textbook_pages.subtitle: Teacher guidance / provisional chapter extract

elements.text:
P1-15-FRESH / fresh
New personal or invented three-event day: coherent first/next/last and before/after explanation; at least one home and one school activity with a plausible day part for each. Must differ from all taught example activity sets; no fixed universal routine. Adult records events/order/contexts/times and explanation, not drawing quality.

P1-15-DELAYED / delayed
Next session, without looking back: invent different home and school activities with plausible day parts; choose a middle event and explain one event before and one after in a coherent three-event story. If across days, name next morning. Assess recall independently; activity/time alternatives accepted with coherent story.

P1-15-Q1 / independent
morning: within the stated day, morning precedes afternoon.

textbook_pages.title: Answer map 5
textbook_pages.subtitle: Teacher guidance / provisional chapter extract

elements.text:
P1-15-Q2 / independent
night: in the stated morning-afternoon-evening-night order; next morning follows night.

P1-15-Q3 / independent
A clearly named or drawn plausible morning activity, e.g. opening curtains at home or greeting a teacher at school; accept different or fictional routines. Do not assess art quality.

P1-15-Q4 / independent
Two distinguishable events in a coherent chosen order, with first/last identified; e.g. take a cup, then put it on a tray. Spoken/acted/card response accepted; story explains order.

textbook_pages.title: Answer map 6
textbook_pages.subtitle: Teacher guidance / provisional chapter extract

elements.text:
P1-15-Q5 / independent
eating, because the locally repeated fictional Amina story says wake, wash, eat, school. Do not impose this order on other families.

P1-15-Q6 / independent
Two events named and a statement that the first happens earlier than the second in the chosen story; e.g. open bag before take out book. Accept coherent fictional alternatives.

S013 / fresh
Both a HOME activity and a SCHOOL activity, each named with a coherent morning/afternoon/evening/night time in the pupil's chosen real OR fictional routine. Accept varied schools and families and an activity in more than one day part. Use new examples rather than repeating the model. Example: fold a cloth at home in the evening; sing at school in the afternoon. Opportunity provided; mastery requires observed response.

textbook_pages.title: Teach, notice and recheck
textbook_pages.subtitle: Teacher guidance / provisional chapter extract

elements.text: Use: Short sessions; read every card aloud, let pupils point, speak or move reachable cards. No clock/calendar knowledge needed. A made-up routine is always allowed. Do not ask for private home information. Drawing quality and handwriting are not time understanding.

Notice: A child may sort by page position, confuse before/after, or think one activity belongs to only one day part. Ask them to act the stated story. Reduce to two cards, say earlier/later, then add a third. Use the book-opening help and new clay recheck on textbook page 10/workbook page 5. Do not give the recheck answer.

Next session: Use workbook page 8, or an exercise book, for P1-15-DELAYED. Require new activities and both contexts with coherent day parts, a middle event and before/after. Record response route, independent/support status, events, order, times and explanation. A practical opportunity is not observed mastery. Reteach only the uncertain part.

Glossary: event: something that happens; before: earlier; after: later; first: start of this story; next: following event; last: end of this story; morning/afternoon/evening/night: named parts of a day in this order. Days repeat: next morning follows night.

lessons.look: Musa lifts an empty bag and a bag with books. Which feels heavier?
lessons.learn: Heavier and lighter compare weight. Size alone does not tell weight. Use small safe objects on a simple balance. The lower pan holds the heavier load.
lessons.worked: On a balance, a stone side goes down and a leaf side goes up. The stone is heavier than the leaf.
lessons.play: With an adult, balance a small stone, eraser and leaf. Predict, compare and order. Lift only light safe items.
lessons.hint: Never ask pupils to lift heavy loads. Use observed results, not appearance.

elements.text: A pan is a dish on a balance. An adult checks that the empty pans are level, move freely and do not touch anything. Use a stable surface within reach. Use only adult-approved light, safe objects.

textbook_pages.title: Teach safely and record honestly
textbook_pages.subtitle: Provisional chapter extract / independent review required

elements.text: Before practical work: an adult approves light safe objects, checks the balance empty and level, free to move, stable, reachable and suited to the loads. Avoid sharp, breakable or choking hazards. No pupil lifts heavy loads. A small smooth stone is a supervised story example, not an instruction to use unsafe stones.

Observe: predict first; one object on each pan; release hands; wait for rest; record lower/higher/level and the comparison. Check pan contact, friction or an unbalanced empty apparatus before interpreting. Record observed results, including equal and predictions that prove wrong. Never award practical mastery from pictures alone. No working balance means practical objective not assessed.

Access and assessment: seated pointing, reachable placement, read-aloud and a scribe writing the pupil's own words may preserve independence. Record person/date/materials/prediction/pan observation/comparison/support. Teaching hints invalidate that attempt as independent: reteach, then use a genuinely new pair without answer help.

Recall: record initial recall before help. Cover help for the new recheck. After two or three school days use another new pair and ask why bigger need not mean heavier. These are opportunities to gather evidence, not observations of mastery.
