lessons.title: Solid shapes around us
lessons.goal: Name and sort cubes, cuboids, cylinders and spheres.
lessons.look: Daniel explores a ball, a box and a closed tin. Which can roll?
lessons.learn: A sphere is ball-shaped. A cube has six equal square faces. A cuboid has six rectangular faces, with opposite faces matching. A cylinder has two flat circular faces and a curved surface.
lessons.worked: A dice models a cube; a cereal box models a cuboid; a closed straight-sided tin models a cylinder; a ball models a sphere.
lessons.play: Sort clean safe objects by solid shape. Test rolling and stacking. Remove sharp tins and small choking hazards.
lessons.hint: A cube is a special cuboid. Use a clear non-cube cuboid for initial comparison.

questions.prompt: What solid does a ball model?
Which solid has six equal square faces?
What solid does a closed straight-sided tin model?
Sort a ball and box by smooth rolling.
questions.answer: Ball rolls smoothly; box does not.
Cube edges are all equal; the chosen non-cube cuboid has unequal adjacent edge lengths.

lessons.title: Flat shapes and patterns
lessons.goal: Match and name circles, squares and rectangles.
lessons.look: Amina traces a box face. How does the flat drawing differ from the box?
lessons.learn: A circle has a curved boundary and no corners. A square has 4 equal straight sides and 4 square corners. A rectangle has 4 square corners and opposite sides equal. A square is a special rectangle.
lessons.worked: Circle, square, circle, square is a repeating pattern. A turned square is still a square.
lessons.play: Trace safe flat faces. Match shapes after turning them. Make a repeating pattern for a pretend cloth border. Find square and rectangular faces in the classroom.
lessons.hint: Orientation does not change a shape. Compare with a non-square rectangle.

questions.prompt: How many corners has a circle?
How many equal sides has a square?

questions.answer: Four right angles, opposite equal sides, unequal adjacent lengths.

questions.prompt: Name an object with a rectangular face.
questions.answer: Suitable example such as a book.

questions.prompt: What stays the same when a square turns?
questions.answer: Its four equal sides and four right-angle corners.

lessons.title: Find out about our class
lessons.goal: Collect and record ages and heights.
lessons.look: The friends discuss how children grow. What could they record respectfully?
lessons.learn: Data are pieces of information. Ask the same question each time. Record age in completed years. Compare heights from floor to head with marked paper strips. Use letters instead of names.
lessons.worked: Invented practice data: pupil A is 6 years, B is 7, C is 6. Two pupils are 6 years old.
lessons.play: Use the invented records or collect voluntary ages privately. Compare paper height strips without ranking children as better or worse. Record height with a consistent method.
lessons.hint: Participation is optional. Do not publish identifiable child data. Fictional data are acceptable.

questions.prompt: How old is practice pupil B?
Order the practice ages from least.
Name a tool for comparing heights.
questions.answer: Marked paper strip or suitable measuring tape

questions.prompt: Why ask everyone the same age question?
questions.answer: To compare answers about the same thing.

supplements.prompt: Mix paper circles and squares, with 3 of one kind and 5 of the other. Sort by shape, name the rule, and count each group.

supplements.teaching_notes: Model sorting by one feature before asking the pupil to sort independently.

supplements.prompt: Sort a mixed collection into 6 blue paper circles, 7 red squares, 8 green triangles and 9 yellow rectangles. Count and order the groups.
supplements.answer: Four correctly classified groups with counts 6, 7, 8, 9, ordered by quantity.
supplements.teaching_notes: The shapes are sorting materials; naming the triangle is not required at P1.

supplements.prompt: Count nine counters once each. Then read cards 1 to 9 in a mixed order chosen by the teacher.
supplements.answer: Nine objects counted exactly once each; each displayed numeral correctly named.
supplements.teaching_notes: Accept spoken number words or the pupil's established accessible communication method.

supplements.prompt: Without copying, write the numerals the teacher says: eight, six, nine, seven.
supplements.answer: 8, 6, 9, 7, recognisable and correctly oriented.
supplements.teaching_notes: Give blank writing space and check that 6 and 9 are not reversed.

supplements.prompt: Find 4 + 5 + 6 and 9 + 0 + 8. Show a counter or count-on check.
supplements.answer: 15 and 17; all three addends included once; correct check.
supplements.teaching_notes: Each addend is 0?9 and each total is ?18.

supplements.prompt: Amina has 4 books and gets 3 more. Musa says 8 books. Check his addition using objects and correct it.
supplements.answer: 4 + 3 = 7; recounting or another valid check shows 8 is wrong.
supplements.teaching_notes: A correct addition total matches all the objects counted once. A wrong total miscounts stock. Check by joining and recounting the sets.

supplements.prompt: There are 9 chalk pieces and 4 are used. Musa says 6 remain. Check with objects and correct him.
supplements.answer: 9 - 4 = 5; 5 + 4 = 9 or a correct take-away check.
supplements.teaching_notes: After taking some objects away, remaining plus removed must equal the starting amount. Use that addition to check the subtraction.

supplements.prompt: Using the teacher's verified genuine Nigerian coin examples or verified official images, point to each coin and say its denomination. Distinguish coins from the book's pretend tokens.
supplements.answer: Each value agrees with the teacher's dated verified denomination checklist; do not infer value from size or token count.
supplements.teaching_notes: Prepare appropriate verified coin examples for the adopted curriculum edition. Pretend value cards alone cannot fulfil this check.

supplements.prompt: With supervision, place an available genuine coin under brown paper and white paper in turn and make a gentle pencil rubbing on each sheet. Say which coin was used.
supplements.answer: Two recognisable surface rubbings made by tracing the coin through the paper; coin and paper intact; stated value matches the example.
supplements.teaching_notes: A rubbing records an existing coin surface through paper. Drawing an invented labelled token is a different task and does not demonstrate coin tracing.

supplements.prompt: Line up one end of three similar paper strips of different lengths. Arrange them shortest to longest and explain.
supplements.answer: Correct physical order after aligned-end comparison; explanation refers to length.
supplements.teaching_notes: Make the strips clearly different and similar in other respects.

supplements.prompt: Measure a table in your hand spans and a short safe path in your footsteps. Record the counts and whose spans/steps were used.
supplements.answer: Equal repeated units without gaps/overlaps; plausible recorded counts labelled with the pupil's unit and measurement.
supplements.teaching_notes: For a seated pupil use repeated personal paper-strip units for a reachable table/path model; record the adaptation.

supplements.prompt: Find three safe similar objects nearby. Compare and order their lengths, then measure one with your own repeated unit.
supplements.answer: Correct local ordering; measurement uses an identified repeated unit consistently.
supplements.teaching_notes: Discuss one use, such as choosing a strip long enough to cover a label.

supplements.prompt: Name one home activity and one school activity. Say whether each happens in your morning, afternoon, evening or night routine.
supplements.answer: Two plausible examples with coherent times, including a school example; accept different family/school routines.
supplements.teaching_notes: Morning, afternoon, evening and night describe parts of a day. A class game may happen at school in the morning; eating an evening meal is a home example.

supplements.prompt: Sort teacher-provided models into cube, non-cube cuboid, cylinder and sphere groups. Explain one choice.
supplements.answer: Each of four solids classified correctly from geometric features; a valid explanation.
supplements.teaching_notes: Use clean large models; rolling alone is insufficient to distinguish all groups.

supplements.prompt: Name or point to a familiar example of a cube, a non-cube cuboid, a cylinder and a sphere.
supplements.answer: Suitable examples for all four, such as dice, rectangular box, straight-sided closed tin and ball.
supplements.teaching_notes: A dice can model a cube, a rectangular box a non-cube cuboid, a straight-sided closed tin a cylinder, and a ball a sphere. Real objects approximate the solids.

supplements.prompt: The teacher shows a square, a non-square rectangle and a circle in mixed orientations. Point to each shape when its name is spoken.
supplements.answer: All three identified correctly, including rotated examples.
supplements.teaching_notes: Turns do not change the defining shape.

supplements.prompt: Match three shape cards to labels square, rectangle and circle. Read or say each name.
supplements.answer: Three correct matches and names.
supplements.teaching_notes: The teacher may read labels aloud; assess shape matching rather than reading proficiency.

supplements.prompt: Compare a square card with a non-square rectangle card. Say one feature shared and one way they differ.
supplements.answer: Both have four square corners; square has four equal sides, non-square rectangle has unequal adjacent lengths.
supplements.teaching_notes: Retain the book's correct statement that a square is a special rectangle.

supplements.prompt: Find or name familiar objects with a square face, a non-square rectangular face and a circular face or outline.
supplements.answer: One suitable example of each; pupil points to the relevant face/outline.
supplements.teaching_notes: A square tile face, a non-square book cover and a round lid show square, rectangular and circular outlines. Name the relevant face or outline, not the whole solid.

supplements.prompt: With consent, ask two willing people their ages in completed years and record letter labels and ages. One may be at home and one at school. If participation is declined, interview a teacher role-playing two people.
supplements.answer: Two consistently asked age questions and accurate letter-labelled records; no names required.
supplements.teaching_notes: Use private voluntary records. A teacher may role-play fictional ages; assess asking and recording rather than merely copying a completed table.

supplements.prompt: With consent, compare two pupils' heights using marked paper strips, then record the strip labels and measurements or comparison results.
supplements.answer: Consistent floor-to-head method; two correctly labelled observations recorded; no claim that taller means better.
supplements.teaching_notes: Offer teacher-provided life-size paper silhouettes when pupils prefer not to be measured.

supplements.prompt: Count aloud from 95 to 105, 125 to 135 and 190 to 200. The teacher may also sample a lower starting point.
supplements.answer: Each one-step sequence correct, including transitions 99/100, 129/130 and 199/200.
supplements.teaching_notes: These are samples of the range, not evidence of a completed 1?200 recital.

supplements.prompt: Read cards 101, 109, 124, 160, 198 and 200 in mixed order.
supplements.answer: Correct number names for every displayed card.
supplements.teaching_notes: Read 109 as one hundred and nine; 190 as one hundred and ninety. Read hundreds, tens and ones in their positions.

supplements.prompt: Share 12 counters first into two equal groups, then regroup into four equal groups. Say how many are in a half and a quarter.
supplements.answer: Two groups of 6; four groups of 3; half is 6 and quarter is 3.
supplements.teaching_notes: Observe actual equal sharing; a written quotient alone is insufficient.

supplements.prompt: Fold a paper rectangle into four equal-area parts. Shade three and name the fraction of the whole shaded.
supplements.answer: Four equal parts, three shaded, named three quarters or 3/4.
supplements.teaching_notes: Three quarters means three of four equal parts of one whole. The whole can be a paper rectangle or a collection of objects.

supplements.prompt: Identify the denomination of each coin and banknote on a teacher-prepared verified checklist for the applicable curriculum edition. Sort coins and notes, then explain how to check a value.
supplements.answer: Every example correctly classified and valued against the teacher's dated authoritative checklist; record any omitted types explicitly.
supplements.teaching_notes: Required denomination inventory and authentic examples must be verified. Pretend cards are arithmetic aids, not evidence of issued money.

supplements.prompt: Two people measure the same table using their own hand spans. Record both results and compare the spans and counts.
supplements.answer: Both counts recorded with whose unit; pupil relates a larger span to potentially fewer units over the same length.
supplements.teaching_notes: Explain that the table did not change when the counts differed.

supplements.prompt: Measure a book in centimetres and a safe classroom distance with a metre strip or tape. Record both readings with units.
supplements.answer: Correct zero alignment, repeated metre units if needed, and plausible cm and m readings.
supplements.teaching_notes: Use physical equipment; printed schematic rulers are not calibrated tools.

supplements.prompt: Why might two hand-span counts disagree, and why should a buyer and maker agree to use centimetres or metres?
supplements.answer: Personal spans vary; agreed standard units have a shared size and allow consistent comparison.
supplements.teaching_notes: State explicitly that a standard unit is agreed in size, rather than simply a longer unit.

supplements.prompt: Arrange all seven weekday cards in the book's Monday-first order. Name them and say what follows the last one.
supplements.answer: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday; Monday follows Sunday.
supplements.teaching_notes: A week is cyclic; accept another declared starting day if the cyclic order is correct.

supplements.prompt: Measure the capacities of three safe containers using the same cup, record cup counts, and physically order containers from least to greatest.
supplements.answer: Consistent equal cupfuls; reliable counts; physical order agrees with measured capacities.
supplements.teaching_notes: Use water with adult supervision and a spill tray, or another suitable safe material.

supplements.prompt: On a cube and a non-cube cuboid, point to every flat face and count without repetition.
supplements.answer: Six faces on each; each counted once using tabs or another reliable method.
supplements.teaching_notes: A face is a flat surface; show the distinction from edges and corners.

supplements.prompt: On a cube and a non-cube cuboid, point to every vertex and count without repetition.
supplements.answer: Eight vertices on each, each counted once.
supplements.teaching_notes: Vertex means corner; point to the meeting point rather than an edge.

supplements.prompt: On a cube and a non-cube cuboid, trace every edge and count without repetition.
supplements.answer: Twelve edges on each; a valid count such as four upper, four lower and four joining.
supplements.teaching_notes: Demonstrate an edge where flat faces meet.

supplements.prompt: Give one familiar cube-shaped object and one non-cube cuboid-shaped object. Identify their faces.
supplements.answer: Suitable examples such as dice and rectangular box; pupil identifies flat faces.
supplements.teaching_notes: Explain that these are approximate real-world models and that cube is a special cuboid.

supplements.prompt: Name a familiar cylinder-shaped object and a sphere-shaped object. Point to their curved surfaces.
supplements.answer: Suitable examples for both; correct recognition of curvature.
supplements.teaching_notes: Examples include a closed straight-sided cylindrical container and a ball.

supplements.prompt: Identify teacher-shown square, non-square rectangle, circle and triangle cards after they have been turned.
supplements.answer: All four named or matched correctly in varied orientations.
supplements.teaching_notes: Use straight-sided triangles and avoid treating orientation as a defining property.

supplements.prompt: Ask four willing people one non-sensitive either/or question, or interview a teacher role-playing four respondents. Record one answer each and build labelled counter rows for the results.
supplements.answer: Four responses obtained and recorded; one counter per answer; aligned rows and labels; total 4.
supplements.teaching_notes: Observe collection as well as the final array; supplied completed counts alone do not test collection.

supplements.prompt: Collect five responses to a three-choice class-game question and sort the records into labelled groups.
supplements.answer: One response recorded per participant; five records correctly grouped into declared categories.
supplements.teaching_notes: A teacher may role-play respondents; no sensitive personal information is needed.

supplements.prompt: Count by ones from 395 to 405, 897 to 905 and 990 to 999. The teacher samples another part of the range if needed.
supplements.answer: Correct successive numbers through each boundary, stopping at 999 for the final sequence.
supplements.teaching_notes: These sampled sequences test range transitions without requiring an exhausting full recital.

supplements.prompt: Explain one situation where counting is useful and another where putting numbers in order is useful.
supplements.answer: Valid counting example, such as checking stock; valid ordering example, such as comparing quantities.
supplements.teaching_notes: Counting establishes how many objects there are. Ordering helps compare quantities or locate values, such as finding the greatest stock total.

supplements.prompt: Put 12 counters together and ring 4. What fraction of the whole collection is ringed? Explain using equal groups.
supplements.answer: 4/12 or 1/3; identifies total 12 and selected 4, or three equal groups with one selected.
supplements.teaching_notes: When four of twelve counters are selected, the fraction is 4/12, equivalent to 1/3. The denominator counts the whole collection; the numerator counts selected counters.

supplements.prompt: On three equal paper rectangles, show halves, thirds and quarters by marking equal-area parts. Label one part on each.
supplements.answer: Respectively 2, 3 and 4 equal-area parts; one part labelled 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4.
supplements.teaching_notes: Check equality of area; equally spaced marks on one edge alone do not ensure a valid full partition.

supplements.prompt: A class records 12 + 7 as 18; another pupil records 1/4 + 2/4 as 3/8. Correct both and explain why accuracy matters when counting supplies or sharing a paper whole.
supplements.answer: 19 and 3/4; wrong totals miscount supplies or misrepresent a fair share; denominator remains 4.
supplements.teaching_notes: Accurate addition gives reliable stock totals and fair combined shares. With like fractions, add the selected equal parts while keeping their size, represented by the denominator, unchanged.

supplements.prompt: A stock of 20 loses 8 items. A paper whole has 3/4 shaded and 1/4 removed. Find both remainders and explain why correct subtraction matters.
supplements.answer: 12 items; 2/4 or 1/2 remains; errors misstate stock or the remaining share.
supplements.teaching_notes: Correct subtraction tells what actually remains in stock or in a shared whole. With like fractions, remove a count of equal parts without changing each part size.

supplements.prompt: Divide 48 by 2 and 30 by 5 using equal groups. Check both with multiplication.
supplements.answer: 24 and 6; 2?24=48 and 5?6=30; equal-group representation.
supplements.teaching_notes: Together with P3-11 questions, this samples every required divisor 2?6 with dividends ?48 and no remainders.

supplements.prompt: Write 24 as a product of two whole-number factors and as a product of three factors greater than one. Check the products.
supplements.answer: Examples 4?6 and 2?3?4; any valid requested products accepted.
supplements.teaching_notes: Products must equal 24; do not repeat the legacy source's erroneous factorisation of 30.

supplements.prompt: Use a ruler to measure every side of a paper square and a tape to measure a safe rectangular tabletop boundary. Add each perimeter with its unit.
supplements.answer: Measured side records agree reasonably with actual objects; every outside side counted once; correct addition and cm/m units.
supplements.teaching_notes: If the tabletop is recorded in cm, also express its perimeter in m using a valid conversion; do not use square units.

supplements.prompt: Two people measure the same safe length using their own arm lengths or hand spans. Compare both personal units and results.
supplements.answer: Both personal measures identified; counts correctly recorded and compared for the same length.
supplements.teaching_notes: People can have different hand spans or arm lengths. Measuring one table with those different units can give different counts even though the table stays unchanged.

supplements.prompt: Compare two people's hand spans and explain why their counts of the same table can differ.
supplements.answer: Pupil identifies different unit lengths and connects smaller units to more repetitions where applicable.
supplements.teaching_notes: A smaller span usually needs more repetitions over the same length than a larger span. Compare both unit sizes before interpreting different counts.

supplements.prompt: Measure a short strip in centimetres and a longer classroom distance in metres. Record both readings and show how the instrument is positioned.
supplements.answer: Correct instrument use and plausible cm/m readings with units; repeated units have no gaps/overlaps.
supplements.teaching_notes: Metre measurement must actually be performed, not merely converted from a supplied number.

supplements.prompt: Use a real labelled calendar or a teacher-prepared month calendar. Point to the 12th and give its day number and month aloud, then write them.
supplements.answer: 12 plus the correct named month from the displayed calendar; year may also be included.
supplements.teaching_notes: Show the month heading; the book's fictional practice month has no month name and cannot alone assess this.

supplements.prompt: Give two examples of how keeping time or using dates helps daily activities. Explain one consequence of ignoring time.
supplements.answer: Suitable examples such as arriving for class, cooking duration or appointments; coherent consequence.
supplements.teaching_notes: Teach usefulness rather than only clock/calendar notation.

supplements.prompt: With supervision, zero a suitable scale. Weigh one light object in grams and another suitable object in kilograms. Record and compare actual readings.
supplements.answer: Correct zero check, safe placement, reasonable readings and units; comparison based on measurements.
supplements.teaching_notes: Do not lift heavy loads. If a scale cannot display both units, use suitable known masses and explicitly record the equipment limitation.

supplements.prompt: With adult supervision, use a graduated plastic jug to measure 1 L of clean water. Pour a second measured 1 L into a safe bucket and state the total.
supplements.answer: Each volume aligned to the correct graduation on a level surface; eye-level reading; total 2 L.
supplements.teaching_notes: Observe practical measuring. This safe jug adapts the source's graduated-cylinder apparatus while retaining the measurement skill.

supplements.prompt: Explain why a 1 L mark must be read accurately when measuring water for an agreed amount. What could happen if the container is tilted?
supplements.answer: Wrong reading gives too much or too little water and defeats the agreed amount; tilt distorts level reading.
supplements.teaching_notes: An inaccurate liquid reading gives too much or too little of an agreed amount. A tilted jug distorts the level reading; use a level surface and eye-height reading.

supplements.prompt: Find an approximately symmetric everyday object, such as a plain rectangular book cover or circular lid. Indicate a possible symmetry line and check with a paper outline.
supplements.answer: Appropriate object and line whose outline halves match; pupil recognises decorative markings may break symmetry.
supplements.teaching_notes: A plain rectangular book-cover outline has mirror lines through opposite side midpoints. A round lid also models symmetry. Printed decoration may break the symmetry of the complete object.

supplements.prompt: Name or point to familiar objects with square, non-square rectangular, triangular and circular outlines. Explain one choice.
supplements.answer: Suitable example for each; correct reference to the outline's defining features.
supplements.teaching_notes: Real objects are approximate shape models; name the relevant face or outline.

supplements.prompt: Find one straight edge and one curved boundary nearby. Trace each in the air and explain the difference.
supplements.answer: Suitable examples, such as a ruler edge and round lid; straight does not bend, curved bends.
supplements.teaching_notes: A ruler edge models a straight line: it does not bend. A round lid boundary models a curve: it changes direction continuously. Look for further familiar examples.
